What Is a Rectovaginal Fistula?

A rectovaginal fistula is an abnormal connection between the rectum and the vagina. Normally, these structures are separate. With a fistula, the abnormal passage can allow material from the rectum to reach the vagina.

The size and location of a fistula can vary. Some may be relatively small, while others can involve a more complicated area of the surrounding tissue.

The term “fistula in women” covers different types of fistulas. A rectovaginal fistula specifically involves the lower digestive tract and vagina.

What Causes a Fistula in Women?

There is no single cause of fistula in women. A healthcare professional may consider several possible contributing factors when evaluating an individual.

Fistula After Childbirth

One possible cause is injury to tissues during childbirth. Complicated or difficult deliveries can sometimes be associated with tissue damage involving the area between the vagina and rectum.

A history of childbirth, particularly when symptoms began after delivery, may therefore be relevant when discussing a possible rectovaginal fistula with a doctor.

Previous Pelvic or Rectal Surgery

Previous surgery involving the rectum, colon, vagina, uterus, or nearby pelvic structures may be considered during an evaluation.

The timing of symptoms in relation to a previous procedure can provide useful information for the treating specialist.

Inflammatory Bowel Conditions

Certain inflammatory bowel conditions, including Crohn’s disease, can be associated with fistula formation. When this is suspected, the broader digestive health history may be considered as part of the assessment.

Infection or Abscess

An infection or abscess in the tissues around the rectum or vagina may also be relevant. If an abnormal passage develops after such a problem, the doctor may investigate whether the two conditions are connected.

Radiation or Other Tissue Injury

Previous radiation involving the pelvic area and certain forms of tissue injury may also be considered when identifying possible causes.

Because several conditions can have similar symptoms, identifying the underlying cause is an important part of planning further care.

What Are the Symptoms of a Rectovaginal Fistula?

Symptoms can vary depending on the location and characteristics of the fistula.

Possible symptoms may include:

  • Passage of gas through the vagina
  • Passage of stool or stool-like material through the vagina
  • Unusual vaginal discharge
  • Unpleasant or unusual odour
  • Irritation around the vaginal or anal area
  • Repeated discomfort in the pelvic or genital region
  • Symptoms that began following childbirth, pelvic surgery, infection, or another relevant event

Not every woman with these symptoms will have a rectovaginal fistula. Similar symptoms can occur with other conditions, which is why an appropriate clinical evaluation is important.

How Is Rectovaginal Fistula Diagnosed?

Diagnosis generally begins with a detailed discussion of symptoms and medical history.

A doctor may ask about:

  • When the symptoms started
  • Whether symptoms followed childbirth or surgery
  • Previous bowel or pelvic conditions
  • Previous infections or procedures
  • Changes in bowel habits
  • The nature and frequency of discharge or leakage

Physical Examination

A pelvic examination and examination of the rectal area may be considered to look for an opening or other findings associated with a fistula.

Additional Tests

Depending on the findings, additional tests may be considered. These can include imaging studies or examinations that provide a closer view of the rectum, vagina, or surrounding pelvic structures.

The choice of testing depends on the suspected location and complexity of the fistula and the individual’s clinical history.

What Is the Treatment for a Rectovaginal Fistula?

Treatment for rectovaginal fistula is not identical for every woman. The approach depends on factors such as the location and size of the fistula, the condition of the surrounding tissue, the underlying cause, previous treatment, and other health considerations.

Addressing the Underlying Cause

When an underlying condition is identified, treatment planning may include managing that condition as part of the overall approach.

For example, a doctor may consider whether inflammation, infection, previous surgery, childbirth-related injury, or another factor is involved.

Observation in Selected Cases

In certain situations, a specialist may discuss observation and supportive management before deciding whether a procedure is appropriate.

This decision is individualized and depends on the characteristics of the fistula and the surrounding tissues.

Surgical Treatment

Surgery may be considered when a fistula persists or when the clinical situation makes repair appropriate.

The specific procedure depends on the location of the fistula and the tissues involved. Surgical approaches may involve closing the abnormal passage and repairing the surrounding tissue.

Some complex cases may require a staged approach rather than a single procedure.

Temporary Diversion in Selected Cases

For certain complex fistulas, a temporary procedure to divert stool away from the affected area may be considered. Whether this is appropriate depends on the individual situation and the surgical plan.

A specialist can explain why a particular approach is being considered and what it involves.

These may include:
